easy.question: What happens when there is a dispute between people?
answers: They go to court
They flee the city
They immediately ask forgiveness
easy.explanation: The passage says that the disputing parties come to judgment so that the judges may decide between them.

easy.question: Who determines the wicked person’s punishment?
answers: The righteous person
The judge
The people
easy.explanation: The passage says that the judge causes the wicked person to be beaten according to his fault.

easy.question: What is the maximum number of stripes mentioned in the passage?
answers: Twenty
Thirty
Forty
easy.explanation: It says, “Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed.”

medium.question: What is the sequence of events described in these verses?
answers: Dispute, judgment, conviction, and punishment
Punishment, dispute, judgment, and acquittal
Judgment, escape, dispute, and punishment
medium.explanation: First there is a dispute; then the parties go to judgment, the judge decides who is righteous and who is wicked, and punishment is given if necessary.

medium.question: What does “according to his fault, by a certain number” mean?
answers: Beating the wicked person without limit
Punishing him according to the seriousness of his guilt
Forgiving the wicked person’s punishment
medium.explanation: The punishment must be proportionate to his guilt and not imposed arbitrarily.

medium.question: In the phrase “then thy brother should seem vile unto thee,” what does “vile” mean?
answers: Rich
Far away
Humiliated or disgraced
medium.explanation: The word means humiliated or disgraced; the warning is not to add extra blows and publicly dishonor the person.

challenge.question: Why does the Torah forbid exceeding forty stripes?
answers: To prevent humiliating and disgracing the person
Because a wicked person may never be punished
Because the judge is not allowed to speak
challenge.explanation: The passage explains that adding more stripes could cause the person to be humiliated and disgraced before everyone.

challenge.question: What can we learn from the fact that the judge must justify the righteous and condemn the wicked before punishment is described?
answers: Both sides must always be punished
Punishment should come only after the case has been examined
There is no need to determine who is guilty
challenge.explanation: The judge first examines the case and determines who is righteous and who is wicked; only then may the guilty person be punished.

challenge.question: What does the description “the judge shall cause him to lie down, and to be beaten before his face” teach about the punishment?

The punishment is carried out secretly without supervision
The punishment takes place within a legal process under the judge’s supervision

easy.question: What animal is mentioned in the verse?
answers: An ox
A donkey
A sheep
easy.explanation: The verse says, “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn.”

easy.question: What must not be done to the ox?
answers: Feed it
Muzzle it
Lead it
easy.explanation: The verse commands that the ox must not be muzzled while it is working.

easy.question: What work is the ox doing in the verse?
answers: Plowing
Transporting goods
Threshing
easy.explanation: The phrase “when he treadeth out the corn” describes the ox’s work of threshing.

medium.question: What is the ox allowed to do while threshing?
answers: Eat some of the grain
Leave the work
Drink from the well
medium.explanation: The prohibition against muzzling it means that the ox should be allowed to benefit from the grain while working.

medium.question: What does the phrase “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox” mean in context?
answers: You must release it from work
You must not prevent it from eating
You must lead it into the field
medium.explanation: In the context of an ox threshing grain, muzzling it means preventing it from eating, usually by covering its mouth.

medium.question: Why is the prohibition mentioned specifically during threshing?
answers: Because the ox is resting and not working
Because the ox is far from the grain
Because the ox is working beside the grain and can eat from it
medium.explanation: While threshing, the ox works among the grain, so it could be prevented from eating.

challenge.question: What moral principle can be inferred from this prohibition?
answers: We should treat fairly those who work and help us
Animals must never be used
All work must be done by hand
challenge.explanation: The verse requires that the ox not be denied a basic benefit while performing its work.

challenge.question: What precise circumstance does the verse emphasize?

The prohibition applies while the ox is threshing
The prohibition applies only before work begins
challenge.explanation: The phrase “when he treadeth out the corn” limits the context to the time when the ox is threshing.

challenge.question: Which understanding is incorrect according to the verse?

The ox may enjoy some grain while working
An ox must never be used for threshing

paragraphs.title: Levirate Marriage and Continuing the Brother’s Name

easy.question: When does the law of levirate marriage apply?
answers: When one brother dies without a son
When the father dies and has a daughter
When a brother leaves the city
easy.explanation: The passage describes brothers living together, when one dies without a son.

easy.question: Whose name will the firstborn child of the brother’s wife carry on?
answers: The woman’s father’s name
The dead brother’s name
The name of the city elders
easy.explanation: The firstborn will succeed in the name of the dead brother so that his name will not be erased from Israel.

easy.question: Where does the widow go if the man does not want to marry her?
answers: To her father’s house
To the sanctuary
To the gate, to the elders
easy.explanation: If the man refuses, the woman goes up to the gate and appeals to the city elders.

medium.question: What happens after the woman announces that the man refuses to marry her?
answers: The city elders call the man and speak with him
She immediately marries another man
The man leaves the city
medium.explanation: After she speaks, the elders call the man and question him about his refusal.

medium.question: In the phrase “let his brother’s wife go up to the gate unto the elders,” who is the woman?
answers: The man’s daughter
The wife of his dead brother
The man’s sister
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the wife of the man’s deceased brother, who goes to the elders when he refuses to marry her.

medium.question: Why is the ceremony of removing the shoe performed?
answers: To celebrate the birth of the firstborn
To punish the city elders
Because the man refuses to build up his brother’s house
medium.explanation: The ceremony takes place after the man refuses to perform the duty of a brother-in-law and build up his brother’s house.

challenge.question: What is the main purpose of continuing the dead brother’s name through the firstborn?
answers: To preserve his memory and the continuation of his name in Israel
To give the living brother a larger inheritance
To move the woman to another city
challenge.explanation: The passage emphasizes that the firstborn will carry on the dead man’s name so that it will not be erased from Israel.

challenge.question: What can we infer from the fact that the procedure takes place at the city gate before the elders?
answers: It is a private matter with no public significance
It is a public and legal procedure before community representatives
Only the woman’s relatives may participate
challenge.explanation: The gate, the elders, and the public ceremony show that the refusal is formally declared before the community.

challenge.question: Which detail of the ceremony especially emphasizes the shame placed on the man who refused?
answers: The firstborn carries the dead brother’s name
The city elders speak with the man
The woman removes his shoe and spits in his face
challenge.explanation: Removing his shoe and spitting in his face are public actions symbolizing condemnation for refusing to build up his brother’s house.

To move the woman to another city
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes that the firstborn will carry on the dead man’s name so that it will not be erased from Israel.

questions.explanation: The gate, the elders, and the public ceremony show that the refusal is formally declared before the community.

answers: The firstborn carries the dead brother’s name

The woman removes his shoe and spits in his face
questions.explanation: Removing his shoe and spitting in his face are public actions symbolizing condemnation for refusing to build up his brother’s house.

paragraphs.title: Limits on Defense During a Fight

easy.question: Who is fighting at the beginning of the passage?
answers: Two men
Two kings
Two women
easy.explanation: The passage describes two men striving and fighting with each other.

easy.question: Who came near to rescue her husband?
answers: His mother
His wife
His sister
easy.explanation: The passage says that “the wife of the one” came near to deliver her husband.

easy.question: What did the woman do to help her husband?
answers: She called for help
She fled the scene
She reached out and seized the attacker’s private parts
easy.explanation: The passage says that she put forth her hand and took the attacker by the secrets.

medium.question: What caused the woman to intervene in the fight?
answers: She wanted to rescue her husband from the attacker
She wanted to punish his brother
She wanted to take the attacker’s property
medium.explanation: She came near because her husband was in danger and she wanted to deliver him from the attacker.

medium.question: In the phrase “taketh him by the secrets,” what is being referred to?
answers: His clothing
His private parts
His hair
medium.explanation: “The secrets” refers to the man’s private parts; the context describes the woman grabbing a sensitive part of his body.

medium.question: What is the sequence of events described in the passage?
answers: The woman was punished, and then the fight began
The woman called for help, and then fled
The men fought, the woman intervened, and then the punishment was commanded
medium.explanation: First there is a fight; then the woman intervenes and grabs the attacker; finally, the law gives the punishment.

challenge.question: Why does the passage end with “thine eye shall not pity her”?
answers: To say that it is forbidden to see the act
To emphasize that the woman was not present
To make clear that the punishment must not be reduced out of pity
challenge.explanation: The phrase emphasizes that the punishment should not be excused or lessened out of pity.

challenge.question: What can we learn from the fact that the woman intended to save her husband but was nevertheless punished?
answers: A good goal does not justify every action
A woman may not rescue her husband
The husband was not in danger
challenge.explanation: Although her goal was to save her husband, the method she used was considered serious and therefore punished.

challenge.question: What unusual detail does the passage emphasize about the woman’s action?
answers: She stood far away from the fight
She grabbed the attacker’s body in a private and sensitive place
She tried to separate two friends
challenge.explanation: The passage specifically says that she seized the attacker’s private parts, rather than merely touching or pushing him away.

To make clear that the punishment must not be reduced out of pity

easy.question: What must not be in a person’s bag?
answers: Different-sized weights
Many coins
Tools
easy.explanation: The passage forbids having a large and a small weight for dishonest measuring.

easy.question: What must not be in the house?
answers: Two bowls
A large measure and a small measure
Two stones
easy.explanation: The passage says not to have different measures, a large one and a small one, in the house.

easy.question: What kind of measure is required according to the passage?
answers: A measure that changes according to the customer
Only a large measure
A perfect and just measure
easy.explanation: The passage commands the use of complete and honest weights and measures.

medium.question: Why is it forbidden to have a large weight and a small weight?
answers: So that people cannot cheat in trade
To save room in the bag
To make them easier to carry
medium.explanation: Two different-sized weights could be used to cheat when measuring goods.

medium.question: In the phrase “divers measures, a great and a small,” what are the measures?
answers: Places to live
Containers or units used to measure volume
Types of stone
medium.explanation: The context concerns a large and a small measuring vessel or unit of volume, not a location.

medium.question: What is promised to those who use complete and honest weights and measures?
answers: Immediate wealth
Victory in war
Longer life in the land
medium.explanation: The passage says that honest weights and measures will enable their days to be lengthened in the land.

challenge.question: What can we infer from the fact that the passage mentions both weights and measures?
answers: Honesty is required in measuring both weight and volume
Cheating is allowed only when selling food
Weights and measures were used for the same purpose
challenge.explanation: Weights were used for weighing and measures for measuring volume, so the prohibition covers different kinds of commerce.

challenge.question: What is the connection between the command to use just measures and the result mentioned in the passage?
answers: The measures determine the size of the house
Honesty is connected with the right to live long in the land
A person who measures correctly does not need to work
challenge.explanation: After commanding the use of honest weights and measures, the passage says this is connected with having long days in the land.

challenge.question: How does the passage describe those who use dishonest measures?
answers: As people who made a harmless mistake
As people who violated only a commercial rule
As an abomination to the Lord and as doing wrong
challenge.explanation: The passage says that such conduct is not merely a commercial mistake but an abomination before the Lord and an act of injustice.

paragraphs.title: Remembering Amalek and Erasing His Memory

easy.question: Who did what is described in these verses to Israel?
answers: Amalek
Egypt
Canaan
easy.explanation: The passage says, “Remember what Amalek did unto thee.”

easy.question: When did Amalek attack Israel?
answers: After the Temple was built
On the way, when Israel came out of Egypt
After entering Jerusalem
easy.explanation: The event happened on the journey, when Israel came out of Egypt.

easy.question: What does the Torah command Israel to do concerning Amalek?
answers: Ask him for peace
Leave the land
Erase his memory and not forget
easy.explanation: The passage commands, “thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek” and “thou shalt not forget it.”

medium.question: Why was Amalek able to attack the weakest people among Israel?
answers: Because the people were faint and weary
Because the people were too heavily armed
Because the people were living in fortified cities
medium.explanation: Amalek attacked those at the rear, who were weak, faint, and weary.

medium.question: What is the sequence of events described in verse 19?
answers: Israel fights Amalek and then leaves Egypt
The Lord gives Israel rest in the land, and then they are commanded to erase Amalek’s memory
Amalek receives an inheritance, and then Israel remembers him
medium.explanation: The command concerning Amalek is given after the Lord has given Israel rest from its enemies and granted it the land.

medium.question: In the phrase “he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee,” what did Amalek do?
answers: He led the entire people
He protected the weak
He attacked those who were at the back of the group
medium.explanation: The context explains that Amalek struck the weak and delayed people who were traveling at the rear.

challenge.question: What does the phrase “he feared not God” emphasize about Amalek’s behavior?
answers: Amalek acted cruelly and without reverence for God
Amalek worshiped the Lord in a special way
Amalek was very afraid of the Israelites
challenge.explanation: The phrase portrays Amalek as acting without fear of God, especially by attacking the weak and weary.

challenge.question: Why is the command to erase Amalek’s memory given only after Israel has rest in the land?
answers: Because Amalek was an ally of Israel
Because the command concerns a time when Israel will be secure in the land and rested from its enemies
Because Israel did not yet know Amalek’s name
challenge.explanation: The passage connects this action with the time when the Lord has given Israel rest from all its enemies and granted it an inheritance.

challenge.question: How can we understand the relationship between “thou shalt not forget it” and “thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek”?
answers: Israel must forget the attack but remember the land
The two commands cancel each other out
Israel must remember the attack and the command, while working to erase Amalek’s name
challenge.explanation: There is no contradiction: Israel remembers what Amalek did and the command it received, while erasing Amalek’s memory itself.

questions.explanation: The phrase portrays Amalek as acting without fear of God, especially by attacking the weak and weary.
